messages.content:
Follow these writing rules. They matter as much as the content:

- Generator scaffolding left in: oaicite, [cite: 1], placeholders -- finish the text and read it
- The "it's not X, it's Y" construction -- just state Y
- A bolded word opening a list item as a per-item tag -- reserve bold for a rare callout
- Saying "is" the long way: serves as, boasts, functions as -- use the plain verb
- One-line dramatic fragments: "That's it. That's the whole thing." -- cut them, the preceding sentence already made the point
- Em dashes clustering in one document -- most drafts need 0-2; use commas, periods or parentheses for the rest
- Filler verbs: leverages, facilitates, unlocks -- use a plain verb, or cut the sentence
- A snake_case identifier written as plain prose -- name it in words, or mark it as inline code
- Marketing cliches: "hidden gem", "let's dive in" -- say the specific thing
- The "Not X. Not Y." listing construction -- state the point once
- Stock section skeleton: "Despite its success", "Looking ahead" -- name the specific thing the section is for
- Standalone filler adverbs: undoubtedly, arguably, notably, importantly, ultimately -- most add nothing; cut them unless one is carrying real emphasis
- A banned synonym of one of this project's canonical terms, per its declared lexicon -- one word, one meaning: use the canonical term the word's own note names
- Dramatic turning points with nothing concrete behind them: "Everything changed." -- name the actual event, or cut it

Now write the following. Return only the requested text.
Write the welcome page new engineers see on their first day at a software company. Around 250 words.

output:
Welcome to the team.

You'll spend your first week getting your laptop set up, meeting your manager, and reading through the docs your team has written for people in exactly your position. Take your time with it. Ask questions in your team channel even if they feel basic — the person who answers you learned the same way, from someone who answered their questions.

Your onboarding buddy will reach out before your start date. They're not your manager and won't be grading you. They're the person you message when you're stuck on something small and don't want to interrupt a meeting to ask.

By the end of week one, you should have your development environment running and have shipped a small, low-risk change to production. We do this on purpose. Shipping something real, even something tiny, teaches you more about how the codebase and the deploy process work than a week of reading would.

Nobody expects you to understand the whole system by Friday. Most engineers here are still learning parts of it years in. If a system looks confusing, it probably is, and the person who wrote it will tell you why if you ask.

We review each other's code, and you should expect the same in return. A review comment is not a judgment of you. It's someone trying to catch a bug before a customer does.

If something in this process is broken, tell your manager. Onboarding gets better because new hires point out what didn't work for them.

Welcome aboard. We're glad you're here.
